_metadata.independence: I read only the brief and the single input file x14-rc-input.json; no other files, repository searches, web or APIs were used.

hints.reason: ROOSTER via crowing at dawn is direct; ALARM via the early wake-up (the rooster as nature's alarm clock) is softer but clicks once seen.

pairs.pair_note: Solid, easy clue; the alarm side leans on the 'nature's alarm clock' idea.

hints.reason: APPLE via the falling-apple legend, FORCE via the newton unit and his laws of motion; both are classic school knowledge.
DOWN completes 'Down Under' and AUSTRALIA is what Down Under names; the phrase is instantly familiar and the pair resolves neatly.

pairs.pair_note: Phrase-join, but a satisfying one since the phrase itself is the nickname.

hints.reason: JUMP via jumper cables / jump-start, BATTERY via the dead battery the cables revive; one clear everyday scene.
BEE via a bee sting, RAY via stingray; both instantly familiar and the double route is tidy.
BOLT via Usain Bolt, the world's fastest sprinter, FLASH via 'the fastest man alive'; a nice person-sense aha, while LIGHTNING would be the plainer double-meaning alternative.

pairs.pair_note: Two good hints exist (FASTEST is the cleverer, LIGHTNING the easier); FASTEST is not weaker.

hints.reason: BOOT via spurs strapped to the boot heel, COWBOY via spurs as iconic cowboy gear.
CAKE and FILE both via the classic file-in-a-cake jailbreak gag; a real aha once the scene lands.
JACK via 'Jack be nimble', CANDLE via the candlestick he jumps; the rhyme is universally known.
WHEEL via 'Ferris wheel', CARNIVAL via the Ferris wheel as the signature carnival ride; very easy but honest on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: Easy phrase-join; fine as a gentle clue.

hints.reason: CHARGE via the bugle 'Charge!' call (also heard at ballgames), CAVALRY via the bugler leading the cavalry in westerns.
CHEF and RAT both via Remy, the cooking rat of Pixar's Ratatouille; the character name is well known, and the obvious alternative RATATOUILLE would contain RAT.

pairs.pair_note: Name recall is a little harder than the film title, but it is a mainstream Pixar lead.

hints.reason: CHRISTMAS via the Nativity ('Away in a Manger'), STABLE via the manger as a stable feeding trough.
CLOTHING via 'The Emperor's New Clothes', NUDE via the emperor parading with nothing on; a fun, PG fairy-tale aha.
CONDUCTOR via the conductor's baton, POLICE via the police baton; a clean double meaning.

COW via the cow jumping over the moon and DISH via the dish running away with the spoon, both in 'Hey Diddle Diddle'; 'diddle' has minor slang senses, but the nursery-rhyme context is dominant (owner may want to confirm comfort).

pairs.pair_note: Nice; note COW is itself a hint in p_milk__moon, which uses the same rhyme, so avoid both on one board.

hints.reason: CUSHION via 'whoopee cushion', JOKE via the whoopee cushion as the archetypal gag; instantly familiar.
DEATH via the Grim Reaper's scythe, WHEAT via the scythe as the old harvest tool; the 'reaper' link makes it satisfying.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; REAPER would also work but SCYTHE is just as good.

hints.reason: DEVIL via 'devil's advocate', LAWYER via advocate as a word for a lawyer; the synonym side is honest and the idiom gives a real second connection.
DREAM via the film's dream-heists, TOP via the spinning-top totem and its famous final shot; widely known film.
hints.fix: TOP: Cobb spins a top to check whether he is dreaming.

pairs.pair_note: Strong film clue; the line 'Cobb's totem' is disputed in the film itself (he says it was Mal's), so the suggested line avoids that.

hints.reason: EGG via ham and eggs / Green Eggs and Ham, RADIO via ham radio; a satisfying double meaning.
MOUNT via 'Mount Rushmore', FACE via the four presidents' faces carved into it.
FEVER via Saturday Night Fever, GREASE via Danny Zuko in Grease; both Travolta's signature roles.
MARKET via 'this little piggy went to market', FOOT via the rhyme being played on a child's toes.
GOLD and STRAW both via Rumpelstiltskin spinning straw into gold; immediately recognizable tale.

pairs.pair_note: Long word but standard spelling; the link is direct.

hints.reason: GREEN via emerald green, IRELAND via the Emerald Isle.
HEAVY via lead as a dense heavy metal ('lead balloon'), PENCIL via pencil lead; the text honestly notes it is graphite.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent, and the text is factually careful.

hints.reason: HOOD via Little Red Riding Hood visiting Grandma, WOLF via the wolf disguised as Grandma.
IVORY via elephant tusks, TRUNK via the elephant's trunk; very easy but honest.
LONDON via the Tower of London, JEWEL via the Crown Jewels kept there; well known to U.S. audiences.
LADDER via the board game Chutes and Ladders, SLIDE via chutes being slides; the synonym side is backed by the game.
MARCH via Julius Caesar and the Ides of March, SALAD via Caesar salad; history plus menu is a real aha.
MASTER via the title 'Jedi Master', YODA via Yoda the famous Jedi; easy but clean.
MILK via dairy cows, MOON via the cow jumping over the moon in 'Hey Diddle Diddle'.

pairs.pair_note: Good; shares a rhyme with p_cow__dish, where COW is a target, so keep them off the same board.

hints.reason: NAIL via nail polish, SHOE via shoe polish; both instantly familiar.

pairs.pair_note: Fine; the NAIL line uses British spelling 'colours'.

hints.reason: NEW and OLD via the New and Old Testaments; one hint naturally summons both halves of the pairing.
hints.fix: NEW: The New Testament follows the Old.

pairs.pair_note: Good; the NEW line's 'it' has no referent when read alone.

hints.reason: SQUASH via spaghetti squash, NOODLE via spaghetti as a noodle; the squash's noodle-like strands tie it together.
PAN via Captain Hook, Peter Pan's nemesis, PIRATE via Hook as pirate captain (and the pirate's hook hand).
PIN via the bobby pin (broad U.S. usage), POLICE via 'bobbies' for British police, a British term but one most Americans know from film and TV.

pairs.pair_note: Judgement call: the police side is British slang, though widely recognized in the U.S.

hints.reason: PLAY via PlayStation, SPACE via space station; both compounds are instantly familiar and the console-plus-ISS pairing is pleasant.

pairs.pair_note: Pure phrase-join but a clean one.

hints.reason: PUNCH via the phrase 'Punch and Judy', PUPPET via it being a puppet show; the show is chiefly a British tradition, so many U.S. players know the phrase without knowing they are puppets.
hints.fix: Punch and Judy is a classic puppet show.

pairs.pair_note: Borderline on U.S. familiarity of the puppet side; the 'seaside' framing in the explanation is British.

hints.reason: SHAKESPEARE via the play Hamlet, TOWN via a hamlet being a tiny settlement; a satisfying double meaning.
SOFT via soft-serve ice cream, TENNIS via the tennis serve; two distinct senses of SERVE.
TIME and TRAVEL both via the Back to the Future DeLorean time machine; the targets form 'time travel', so one reference covers both.

pairs.pair_note: Fun pop-culture clue; the two targets are really one compound, which makes it easy.
